pod.e: Origin uncertain. Perhaps from Middle English *pod ("seed-pod, husk, shell, outer covering"; attested in pod-ware (“legume seed; seed grain”)), itself possibly from Old English pād (“an outer garment, covering, coat, cloak”), from Proto-West Germanic *paidu, from Proto-Germanic *paidō (“coat, smock, shirt”).
pod.g: A self-contained unit, container, or enclosure that holds, protects, or transports something.

poet.e: From Middle English poete, from Old French poete, from Latin poēta (“poet, author”), from Ancient Greek ποιητής (poiētḗs, “creator, maker, author, poet”), from ποιέω (poiéō, “to make, compose”).

point.e: From Middle English poynt, from Old French point m (“dot; minute amount”), from Latin pūnctum (“a hole punched in; a point, puncture”), substantive use of pūnctus m, perfect passive participle of pungō (“to prick, punch”); alternatively, from Old French pointe f (“sharp tip”).
From Middle English pointen, poynten, by apheresis of apointen, appointen, appoynten.

pointless.e: From Middle English pointles, poynteles, poyntlees. By surface analysis, point + -less.
pointless.g: Having no point or sharp tip; terminating squarely or in a rounded end.

poise.e: From Middle English poys, poyse, from Anglo-Norman pois, Middle French pois (“weight”) and Anglo-Norman poise, Middle French poise (“measure of weight”), from Latin pendere (“to weigh, ponder, think”).
poise.g: A state of balance, equilibrium or stability.

poise.e: From French physicist and physiologist Jean Léonard Marie Poiseuille.
poise.g: Unit of viscosity in the centimetre–gram–second system of units (CGS).

poison.e: From Middle English poysoun, poyson, pusoun, from Old French poison, poisun, from Latin pōtiōnem (“drink, a draught, a poisonous draught, a potion”), from pōtō (“to drink”). Mostly displaced native Old English ātor and lybb.
poison.g: A substance that is harmful or lethal to a living organism when ingested.

poisonous.e: From Middle English poisounous, poysonouse. By surface analysis, poison + -ous.
poisonous.g: Containing sufficient poison to be dangerous to touch or ingest.

pole.e: English poleFrom Middle English pole, pal, from Old English pāl (“a pole, stake, post; a kind of hoe or spade”), from Proto-West Germanic *pāl (“pole”), from Latin pālus (“stake, pale, prop, stay”), perhaps from Old Latin *paxlos, from Proto-Italic *pākslos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂ǵ- (“to nail, fasten”).
pole.g: Originally, a stick; now specifically, a long and slender piece of metal or (especially) wood, used for various construction or support purp

pole.e: From Middle French pole, pôle, from Latin polus, from Ancient Greek πόλος (pólos, “axis of rotation”).
pole.g: Either of the two points on the earth's surface around which it rotates; also, similar points on any other rotating object.

policy.e: From Middle English policie, from Old French policie, pollicie and police, from Late Latin politia (“citizenship; government”), classical Latin polītīa (in Cicero), from Ancient Greek πολιτεία (politeía, “citizenship; polis, (city) state; government”), from πολίτης (polítēs, “citizen”).
policy.g: A principle of behaviour, conduct which an entity (government, organization, etc.) applies or seeks to follow, especially as formally expres

policy.e: From Middle French police, from Italian polizza, from Medieval Latin apodissa (“receipt for money”), from Ancient Greek ἀπόδειξις (apódeixis, “proof, declaration”).

polish.e: From Middle English polishen, from Old French poliss-, stem of some of the conjugated forms of polir, from Latin polīre (“to polish, make smooth”), from Proto-Indo-European *pelh₂- (“to drive, strike, thrust”), from the notion of fulling cloth.

poll.e: From Middle English pol, polle ("scalp, pate"), from or cognate with Middle Dutch pol, pōle, polle (“top, summit; head”), from Proto-West Germanic *poll, from Proto-Germanic *pullaz (“round object, head, top”), from Proto-Indo-European *bolno-, *bōwl- (“orb, round object, bubble”), from Proto-Indo-European *bew- (“to blow, swell”).
poll.g: A survey of people, usually statistically analyzed to gauge wider public opinion.

poll.e: Perhaps a shortening of Polly, a common name for pet parrots.

pollute.e: From Middle English polluten, borrowed from Latin pollūtum, from pollūtus (“no longer virgin", "unchaste”), perfect passive participle of polluō (“soil", "defile", "dishonor”).
pollute.g: To make something harmful, especially by the addition of some unwanted product.

pollution.e: From Middle English pollucioun, pollucion (“desecration, impurity”), from Anglo-Norman pollutiun, Middle French pollution, pollucion, and their source, post-classical Latin pollūtiō (“defilement, desecration; nocturnal emission”) (4th century), from the participial stem of polluō (“to soil, defile, contaminate”).
pollution.g: Physical contamination, now especially the contamination of the environment by harmful substances, or by disruptive levels of noise, light e

pomegranate.e: Pōmum is possibly ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *h₂po-h₁ém-os (“taken off”) (in the sense of being picked off a plant), from *h₂epó (“away; off”) + *h₁em- (“to distribute; to take”); while grānātum is derived from grānātus (“having many grains or seeds”).
pomegranate.g: The fruit of the Punica granatum, about the size of an orange with a thick, hard, reddish skin enclosing many seeds, each with an edible pin

pommel.e: From Middle English pomel, from Old French pomel and Medieval Latin pomellum, pumellum, presumedly via Vulgar Latin *pomellum (“ball, knob”), the diminutive of Late Latin pōmum (“apple”).
pommel.g: The upper front brow of a saddle.

pomp.e: From Middle English pompen. Possibly an alteration of pampen (English pamp), from Middle Low German pampen (“to pamper oneself, live luxuriously”), from Old Saxon *pampōn, from Proto-Germanic *pampōną (“to swell”), from Proto-Indo-European *bamb- (“round object”).

pomposity.e: From Middle English pomposite (“solemnity”), from Latin pompōsitās. By surface analysis, pomp + -osity.
pomposity.g: The quality of being pompous; self-importance.

pond.e: From Middle English pond, ponde (“pond, pool”), probably from Old English *pond, *pand (attested in placenames), a variant of *pund (“enclosure”).
pond.g: An inland body of standing water, either natural or man-made, that is smaller than a lake.

ponder.e: From Middle English ponderen, from Old French ponderer (“to weigh, balance, ponder”) from Latin ponderāre (“to weigh, ponder”), from pondus (“weight”), from pendere (“to weigh”); see pendent and pound.

pool.e: From Middle English pool, pole, pol, from Old English pōl (“pool”), from Proto-West Germanic pōl, from Proto-Germanic *pōlaz (“pool, pond”), from Proto-Indo-European *bōlos (“bog, marsh”). For the meaning development to a supply of resources compare typologically Russian пруд пруди́ (prud prudí) (< пруд (prud)).
pool.g: A small and rather deep area of (usually) fresh water, as one supplied by a spring, or occurring in the course of a stream or river; a reser

pool.e: From French poule (“collective stakes in a game”). The French word "poule" in this context is an abbreviation of "poulain, pouliche" (foal, filly), and referred to races with female horses under 3 years old. It then became used by punters to designate bets on that race, and started to be used from the racetrack to the stadiums. 2.

poor.e: From Middle English povre, povere, from Old French and Anglo-Norman povre, poure, from Latin pauper, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂w- (“few, small”). Displanced native wantsome, Middle English unlede (“poor”, from Old English unlǣde), Middle English unweli, unwely (“poor, unwealthy”.
poor.g: With no or few possessions or money, particularly in relation to contemporaries who do have them.

poorly.e: From Middle English poorly, pouerly, poreliche, poureliche, pouerliche, equivalent to poor + -ly.
poorly.g: In a poor manner or condition; without plenty, or sufficiency, or suitable provision for comfort.

poplar.e: From Middle English popler, from Anglo-Norman popler and Old French poplier (compare French peuplier), from Latin pōpulus, with a suffix later added.
poplar.g: Any of various deciduous trees of the genus Populus.

populate.e: Borrowed from Medieval Latin populātus, past participle of populor (“populate”), from Latin populus (“people”).
populate.g: To supply with inhabitants; to people.

population.e: Borrowed from Late Latin populatio (“a people, multitude”), as if a noun of action from Classical Latin populus, equivalent to populate + -ion.
population.g: The people living within a political or geographical boundary.

populous.e: First used in English in the mid 15th century; from Latin populosus (“full of people, populous”).

porch.e: From Middle English porche, from Old French, from Latin porticus (“portico”).
porch.g: A covered entrance to a building, whether taken from the interior, and forming a sort of vestibule within the main wall, or projecting witho

pore.e: From Middle English pore, from Old French pore, from Latin porus, from Ancient Greek πόρος (póros, “passage”).
pore.g: A tiny opening in the skin.

pore.e: From Middle English poren, pouren, puren (“to gaze intently, look closely”), from Old English *pūrian, from Proto-West Germanic *pūrōn, suggested by Old English spyrian (“to investigate, examine”).
pore.g: To study meticulously; to go over again and again.

porphyry.e: From Old French porfire, from Ancient Greek πορφυρίτης λίθος (porphurítēs líthos, “purple stone”), from πορφύρα (porphúra, “purple-fish, purple dye”).
porphyry.g: A hard igneous rock consisting of large crystals in a fine-grained matrix.

port.e: From Old English port, borrowed from Latin portus (“port, harbour”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pértus (“crossing”) (and thus a distant doublet of ford).
port.g: A place on the coast at which ships can shelter, or dock to load and unload cargo or passengers.

port.e: From Old French porter, from Latin portāre (“carry”).
port.g: To carry, bear, bring, or transport. See porter.

portent.e: Borrowed from Latin portentum, participle of portendere, from portendō (“to predict, to foretell”).
portent.g: Something that portends an event about to occur, especially an unfortunate or evil event; an omen.

porter.e: From Middle English porter, portere, portier, borrowed from Anglo-Norman portour and Old French porteor, from Late Latin portātor, from past participle of Latin portāre (“to carry”). By surface analysis, port (“to carry”) + -er.
porter.g: A person who carries luggage and related objects; (historically) one who carried luggage or did manual labour in the transloading of cargo.

porter.e: From Middle English porter, portere, portare, borrowed from Anglo-Norman portour and Old French portier, from Late Latin portarius (“gatekeeper”), from Latin porta (“gate”).
porter.g: A person in control of the entrance to a building.

portico.e: From Italian portico, from Latin porticus (“porch”), from porta (“gate”).
portico.g: A porch, or a small space with a roof supported by columns, serving as the entrance to a building.

portion.e: From Middle English porcioun, borrowed from Old French porcion, accusative of Latin portiōnem (“a share, part, portion, relation, proportion”), from portiō, akin to pars (“part”); see part.

portray.e: From Middle English portray, from Middle French portraire.
portray.g: To paint or draw the likeness of.

pose.e: From Middle English pose, from Old English ġeposu pl (“cold in the head; catarrh”, literally “(the) sneezes; (the) snorts”), from Old English pos, ġepos (“sneeze, snort”), from Proto-West Germanic *pos, from Proto-Germanic *pusą (“sneeze, snort”), from Proto-Germanic *pusōną, *pusjaną (“to snort, blow”), from *pus- (“to blow, breathe hard”).

From Middle English posen, from Old French poser (“to put, place, stell, settle, lodge”), from Vulgar Latin pausāre (“to blin, cease, pause”), from Latin pausa (“pause”), from Ancient Greek παῦσις (paûsis); influenced by Latin pōnere.
pose.g: To place in an attitude or fixed position, for the sake of effect.

position.e: From Middle English posicioun, from Old French posicion, from Latin positiō (“a putting, position”), from positus (“placed, situated”), past participle of pōnō (“to place”); see ponent.

possess.e: From Middle English possessen (“to have, own; to obtain possession of; to inhabit, occupy”), from Middle French possesser, possessier, Old French possesser, possessier (“to have, own, possess; to dominate”), from Latin possessus (“possessed; seized”), the perfect passive participle of possideō (“to have, hold, own, possess; to have possessions.
possess.g: To have (something) as, or as if as, an owner; to have, to own.

possession.e: From Latin possessiō, possessiōnis. Equivalent to possess + -ion.
possession.g: A control or occupancy of something for which one does not necessarily have private property rights.

possible.e: From Middle English possible, from Old French possible, from Latin possibilis (“possible”), from posse, possum (“to be able”); see power.
possible.g: Able but not certain to happen; neither inevitable nor impossible.

post.e: From Middle English post, from Old English post (“pillar, door-post”) and Old French post (“post, upright beam”), both from Latin postis (“door, post, doorpost”).
post.g: A long dowel or plank protruding from the ground; a fencepost; a lightpost.

post.e: Borrowed from Middle French poste, from Italian posta (“stopping-place for coaches”), feminine of posto (“placed, situated”).
post.g: Each of a series of men stationed at specific places along a postroad, with responsibility for relaying letters and dispatches of the monarc

posterity.e: Late 14th century, from Middle French posterité, from Latin posteritas, from posterus (“following, coming after”), from post (“after”) (English post-).
posterity.g: All the future generations, especially the descendants of a specific person.

pot.e: From Middle English pot, potte, from Old English pott (“pot”) and Old French pot (“pot”) (probably from Frankish *pott); both Old English and Frankish from Proto-Germanic *puttaz (“pot, jar; tub”), of unknown origin. Middle English pot gave rise to Irish pota, Scottish Gaelic poit, and Welsh pot through borrowing.
pot.g: A flat-bottomed vessel (usually metal) used for cooking food, possibly excluding saucepans (see usage notes).

pot.e: Possibly a shortened form of Mexican Spanish potiguaya or potaguaya (“cannabis leaves”), from pota + de + guaya (see guayar (“to lament”)), or from potación de guaya (literally “drink of grief”), supposedly denoting a drink of wine or brandy in which marijuana buds were steeped.

potsherd.e: From Middle English pot-sherd, pot-schord, pot scherd, pot scarth, from Middle English pot, pote, potte (“a container, pot, vessel; especially an earthenware vessel”) (from late Old English pot, pott (“a pot”), from Proto-Germanic *puttaz (“pot, jar; tub”), of unknown origin) + Middle English sherd (“piece of fired clay or broken earthenware.
potsherd.g: A piece of ceramic from pottery, often found on an archaeological site.

pottage.e: From Middle English pottage, from Anglo-Norman and Old French potage, equivalent to pot + -age.
pottage.g: A thick soup or stew, made by boiling vegetables, grains, and sometimes meat or fish, a staple food throughout Europe in the Middle Ages.

potter.e: From Middle English pottere, from Old English pottere (“potter”, in placenames), from Proto-West Germanic *pottārī (“pot-maker”), equivalent to pot + -er. Influenced by Anglo-Norman poter, Old French potier (“potter”).
potter.g: One who makes pots and other ceramic wares.

potter.e: Frequentative of pote, equivalent to pote + -er.
potter.g: To act in a vague or unmotivated way; to fuss about with unimportant things.

pottery.e: From Old French poterie, from potier (“potter”), from the root of pot, equivalent to pot + -ery.
pottery.g: Fired ceramic wares that contain clay when formed.

pouch.e: From Middle English pouche, poche, borrowed from Old Northern French pouche, from Old French poche, puche (whence French poche; compare also the Anglo-Norman variant poke), of Germanic origin: from Frankish *poka (“pouch”) (compare Middle Dutch poke, Old English pohha, dialectal German Pfoch).
pouch.g: A small bag usually closed with a drawstring.

poultice.e: From Middle English pultes, from Latin pultes, plural of puls. The phonological development from Middle English is regular; compare poultry.
poultice.g: A soft, moist mass, usually wrapped in cloth and warmed, that is applied topically to a sore, aching or lesioned part of the body to soothe

poultry.e: From Middle English pultrie, from Old French pouleterie, from poulet, diminutive of poule (“hen”), from Latin pullus (“chick”). By surface analysis, poult + -ry. For the development of Middle English /u/ to modern /oʊ/, /əʊ/ before /lt/, /ld/, /ln/, compare boult, boulder, colter/coulter, poultice, shoulder, won't.
poultry.g: Domestic fowl (e.g. chickens, ducks, turkeys, geese) raised for food (meat, eggs, or both).

pounce.e: From French ponce, from Latin pūmex.
pounce.g: A type of fine powder, as of sandarac, or cuttlefish bone, sprinkled over wet ink to dry the ink after writing or on rough paper to smooth t

pounce.e: From Middle English pounce, probably akin to punch. Possibly from Old French ponchonner (compare French poinçonner).

pound.e: From Middle English pound, from Old English pund (“a pound, weight”), from Proto-West Germanic *pund, from Proto-Germanic *pundą (“pound, weight”), an early borrowing from Latin pondō (“by weight”), ablative form of pondus (“weight”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pend- (“to pull, stretch”).
pound.g: A unit of weight in various measurement systems.

pound.e: From Middle English pounde, ponde, pund, from Old English *pund (“an enclosure”).
pound.g: A place for the detention of stray or wandering animals.

pour.e: From Middle English pouren (“to pour”), of uncertain origin. Perhaps from Old Northern French purer (“to sift (grain), pour out (water)”), from Latin pūrō (“to purify”), from pūrus (“pure”). To pour displaced several Middle English verbs: schenchen, schenken (“to pour”), from Old English sċenċan (“to pour out”) and Old Norse skenkja.
pour.g: To cause (liquid, or liquid-like substance) to flow in a stream, either out of a container or into it.

poverty.e: From Middle English poverte, from Old French poverté (Modern French pauvreté), from Latin paupertās, from pauper (“poor”) + -tas (“noun of state suffix”).
poverty.g: The quality or state of being poor; lack of money

powder.e: From Middle English poudre, pouder, pouldre, borrowed from Old French poudre, poldre, puldre, from Latin pulverem, accusative singular of Latin pulvis (“dust, powder”).
powder.g: The fine particles which are the result of reducing a dry substance by pounding, grinding, or triturating, or the result of decay; dust.

power.e: From Middle English power, poer, from Old French poeir, from Vulgar Latin potēre, from Latin posse, whence English potent.
power.g: The ability to do or undergo something.

powerful.e: From Middle English pouerful, powarfull. By surface analysis, power + -ful.
powerful.g: Having, or capable of exerting, power or influence.

powerless.e: From Middle English pouerles, powerles, equivalent to power + -less.
